summary: Find the minimum number of days to wait so that m bouquets of k adjacent bloomed flowers can be made, or -1.
mainInsight: Waiting longer never hurts, so 'can make m bouquets by day d' is monotone in d. Binary search the day and test each candidate with a greedy scan counting runs of k bloomed flowers.
invariant: lo is infeasible or the smallest candidate, hi is always feasible, and the first feasible day lies in [lo, hi].
canonicalApproach: Binary search on days with greedy check

approaches.name: Test every day
approaches.summary: For each day in order, run the greedy check.

approaches.name: Binary search on days with greedy check
approaches.summary: Search the minimal day with bouquets(day) >= m.

personalSolution.approach: Binary search on days with a greedy adjacency scan and an ans variable
personalSolution.notes: Optimal. The commented-out m * k > n guard is a good O(1) early exit that you can keep.

commonMistakes: Not resetting the run after forming a bouquet.
Forgetting the impossibility case (m * k > n).
Counting bloomed flowers instead of adjacent runs.
Overflow of m * k in 32-bit languages.
edgeCases: All flowers bloom on the same day.
A single late flower splits runs.

promptVariants: Why can you binary search on the number of days?
What property of the days makes the feasibility test monotone?
cards.answer: If m bouquets can be made after d days, they can also be made after d + 1 days, because flowers never un-bloom. So the feasibility predicate is false for small d and true from some day onward, and we want the first true day. Each test is a greedy left-to-right scan that forms a bouquet whenever k adjacent flowers have bloomed.
cards.explanation: Binary search on the answer needs a monotone yes/no check that is cheap to evaluate.

promptVariants: Why does your feasibility scan reset `adjacency` to 0 after counting a bouquet?
What would happen in your makeBouquets if adjacency were not reset after a bouquet?
cards.answer: A flower can belong to only one bouquet, so after k adjacent flowers form a bouquet the run must start over. Without the reset, the count would reach k + 1, k + 2, ... and never equal k again, so at most one bouquet would be counted in a long run of bloomed flowers.
keyPoints: Without reset only one bouquet per run
cards.explanation: Greedy: forming a bouquet as soon as possible never hurts the later flowers.

promptVariants: For bloomDay = [1, 2, 9, 3, 4, 9, 5, 6], m = 2, k = 3, why is returning the 6th smallest day (6) wrong?
Why can't the answer be the (m * k)-th smallest bloom day?
options: Bloomed flowers must be adjacent, and on day 6 they form runs of length 2 only
Bloomed flowers must be distinct, and day 6 repeats a day from earlier flowers
The sixth smallest day is smaller than the largest bloom day among all flowers
A bouquet needs one flower from each of the days sorted in increasing order
cards.answer: Bloomed flowers must be adjacent, and on day 6 they form runs of length 2 only
cards.explanation: On day 6 six flowers have bloomed but the two 9s split them into runs of 2, 2 and 2, so no bouquet of 3 adjacent flowers exists. The first day with two runs of 3 is day 9.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Bloomed flowers must be distinct, and da: Bloom days may repeat; distinctness is not required.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The sixth smallest day is smaller than t: That is true but irrelevant; the answer is not constrained to be the largest day.
incorrectOptionExplanations.A bouquet needs one flower from each of: A bouquet is any k adjacent bloomed flowers, regardless of their days.

promptVariants: When does the problem return -1, and how can you detect it before searching?
What is the cheap impossibility test for this problem?
cards.answer: It returns -1 exactly when m * k > n, because even when every flower has bloomed we can make only n // k bouquets. Checking this first avoids a search whose upper bound is not feasible; in a fixed-width language also compute m * k with a 64-bit type because m and k can multiply beyond 32 bits.
keyPoints: On the last day all flowers are bloomed
Check first; beware overflow of m * k
cards.explanation: The test is also what guarantees that hi = max(bloomDay) is a feasible upper bound.

cards.explanation: The binary search over [min, max] takes about log D iterations and each runs the O(n) greedy scan.

incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n * D): That would test every day in turn instead of halving the range.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(n log n): There is no sorting; the search range is the day values, not the array size.
incorrectOptionExplanations.O(log D): Each iteration still scans all n flowers.

promptVariants: The binary search and the greedy scan use only a few integers, so the extra space is O(___).
Your search uses lo, hi = 1, max(days) with an ans variable. How does it differ from the lo < hi template, and what is the trade-off?
Compare the 'record the answer' template with the 'shrink to the first true' template.
cards.answer: Your version loops while lo <= hi and records ans whenever the check passes, returning -1 if it never does, so it needs no separate impossibility test. The lo < hi version needs the m * k > n guard first, but ends with lo exactly at the first feasible day and has a tighter range [min, max]. Both are O(n log D).
keyPoints: lo < hi converges to the first true
cards.explanation: Pick one template and use it consistently; mixing them is a common source of off-by-one errors.
